query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An ML‐optimized SPS processing schedule, which tailors rapid heating and controlled cooling to maximize interfacial diffusion, will yield a W–Cu composite that is more uniform and has fewer voids than the current vapor‐coated sintered baseline, leading to improved thermal transport and mechanical durability under fusion‐reactor irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix that currently show interfacial heterogeneity and void/defect issues from conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Apply a machine learning–derived SPS (spark-plasma sintering) protocol that optimizes temperature gradients, ramp rates, and cooling times to enhance interfacial bonding without melting the W.
generation.conditions: Processing under an SPS regime where the Cu is near or in the molten state while W remains solid, and service conditions are equivalent to high heat flux and irradiation environments typical of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, defect‐free interfacial diffusion layer between W and Cu achieved through optimized rapid heating and controlled cooling, resulting in minimal voids and phase separation.
generation.mechanism: The ML model, trained with data from vapor‐coated sintered samples and other SPS experiments, predicts an optimal processing window that promotes atomic interdiffusion and oxide layer removal at the W–Cu interface. This tailored process reduces void and defect formation while preserving the distinct high-melting W and low-melting Cu characteristics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the vapor‐coated sintered baseline, the ML‐optimized composite will exhibit statistically lower void density, better interfacial continuity, enhanced thermal conductivity, and maintained or improved mechanical strength under irradiation.
generation.baseline: The current vapor‐coated W powders sintered to near-perfect contact between constituents, which nevertheless suffer from some degree of phase inhomogeneity and defect-related limitations.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable during SPS processing (where temperature control prevents melting W or boiling Cu) and is designed for service conditions that include high thermal flux and irradiation typical in fusion reactor joint applications.
generation.uncertainty: While the ML-optimized processing window is expected to reduce defects, the precise parameters and long-term resistance to irradiation-induced degradation require further experimental validation in both lab-scale SPS trials and simulated service environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set using the conventional vapor-coated sintering process and another set using the ML-optimized SPS protocol. Subject both sample sets to identical thermal cycling and simulated irradiation conditions representative of fusion-reaction environments.
measurements: Quantification of void density and interfacial microstructure via SEM/TEM image analysis
Thermal conductivity measurements using standard techniques
Mechanical testing (e.g., compressive/tensile strength) before and after irradiation simulation
Comparative phase analysis via XRD to detect unintended phase separation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-optimized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in void density and an improvement in both thermal conductivity and mechanical durability when compared with the conventional vapor-coated baseline, or if they exhibit additional processing-induced defects, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The unique design concept of HEAs can be applied to the innovation of a new generation of powder superalloys and the development of turbine disk components suitable for the extreme working conditions of the aero-engine. Combining MA (mechanical alloying) with SPS (spark plasma sintering) to prepare HEAs has recently received much attention. MA overcomes phase diagram limitations by using mechanical energy to effect the atomic alloying of solid components, producing alloy systems inaccessible to conventional procedures and increasing powder homogeneity and solid solubility. SPS is a new rapid sintering technology commonly used to prepare high-performance HEA blocks. It combines plasma activation and hot-pressing sintering and benefits from fast heating and cooling rates, short sintering times, controllable microstructures, energy savings, and low environmental impact. Pulse current heating and high pressure can rapidly heat and sinter the powder particles into sintered blocks [,,]. In the current work, AZ91 metal matrix composites reinforced with 10 wt% of HEA particles were fabricated by spark plasma sintering process. AZ91–SiC composites were also synthesized for comparison of their mechanical properties. Microstructure and mechanical properties of the sintered composites were studied and the following conclusions could be drawn:AZ91–HEA composite with a uniform distribution of HEA particles in the matrix could be manufactured using spark plasma sintering process. The composite consisted of α-Mg, Mg17Al12 and FCC phase. Phase transformation was not observed in the sintered composite compared to the as-milled powder. No reaction layer was formed in the interfacial region between HEA and α-Mg matrix.The addition of HEA efficiently enhances hardness and compressive yield strength (C.Y.S) of AZ91–HEA. After adding HEA particles, hardness and C.Y.S of the composite were increased by 48% and 17%, respectively.In AZ91–HEA composite, thermal mismatch effect, load transfer effect and grain-refinement effect contributed to the increment in yield strength. frame.system: A composite system built from tungsten (W) particles or interconnected W regions embedded within a copper (Cu) matrix, intended for high-heat-transfer applications in fusion‐reactor joints under irradiation.
frame.goal: To achieve a uniform, defect‐free W–Cu interface that maximizes thermal transport properties while preserving mechanical durability under service conditions.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing techniques (e.g., induction/arc-plasma casting, Cu infiltration into W skeletons, spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, vapor coating, and metal 3D printing) tend to lead to phase separation, void formation, and interfacial defects, which impair thermal performance and/or compromise mechanical strength.
root_cause_cues: filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects
spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids
constraints: a single intervention must overcome the previous limitations
the processing must begin with W particles or preconnected W regions within a Cu matrix
the solution must preserve mechanical durability under irradiation
service conditions are those relevant for high heat flux and irradiation in fusion-reactor joints
regime: processing regime where Cu is molten (or near melting) but W remains solid
service regime under irradiation and thermal cycling typical of fusion reactor environments
prior_attempts: Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder, which can leave defects
Spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying that produce fine, uniform structures but also voids
Vapor-coating of W powders followed by sintering to enhance contact
Metal 3D printing approaches that have been explored but not yet optimized

families.principle: Leverage data analytics and machine learning to correlate historical and experimental processing data with interfacial quality, thereby optimizing processing parameters that result in uniform, defect‐free interfaces.
cues_for: limitations of conventional processing techniques (e.g., spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, vapor coating, metal 3D printing)
the need to overcome phase separation and void formation in a systematic, optimized manner
cues_against: The extreme processing conditions (Cu molten while W remains solid, and service under irradiation) may limit the available training data and complicate the model’s predictive accuracy.
families.best_lever: Develop an ML model that predicts the optimal processing window (e.g., tailored temperature gradients, controlled cooling rates) which minimizes voids and defects while maximizing interfacial contact, using the performance of vapor-coated sintered samples as a baseline for comparison.

families.principle: Develop in situ, high-resolution experimental techniques to monitor the formation of W–Cu interfaces and detect the transient generation of voids or defects during processing under extreme conditions and irradiation.
cues_for: processing in a molten Cu regime under irradiation (challenging conditions)
cues_against: The central question calls for a single processing intervention to overcome limitations rather than primarily a diagnostic tool, even though improved measurement is essential for validation.
families.best_lever: Implement advanced synchrotron or in situ electron microscopy during processing to directly observe interface formation so that processing parameters can be real‐time adjusted to avoid the conditions leading to voids.

families.principle: Use atomistic simulations and refined interatomic potentials to predict interfacial energies and wetting behavior in the extreme processing conditions (Cu molten, W solid) so as to minimize phase separation and void formation.
cues_against: Several experimental fabrication techniques (e.g., spark‐plasma sintering, vapor coating, metal 3D printing) have already been attempted, suggesting that a simulation alone might not directly yield the processing intervention.
families.best_lever: Develop and validate a new interatomic potential for the W–Cu system under high-temperature gradients to simulate and predict optimal interfacial wetting regimes, then use these insights to guide a targeted processing window.

families.principle: Apply enhanced sampling or free energy calculation techniques to map the thermodynamic landscape of the W–Cu interface formation, identifying processing temperature ranges and conditions that minimize the free energy penalties associated with voids and defects.
cues_against: The existing description emphasizes a single physical intervention in the processing method rather than only a computational insight about free-energy barriers.
families.best_lever: Use advanced free energy methods to pinpoint a narrow processing regime where the interfacial free energy difference is minimized, guiding a specific processing parameter, such as a controlled thermal profile, to promote complete wetting and defect-free interfaces.
